items.title: [cbc.ca] B.C. floods force evacuations, shelter orders as roads close
items.content_html:
🌲 ✏️

Heavy rain and flooding across British Columbia’s South Coast prompted shelter-in-place advisories near Squamish and in Pemberton Valley, while evacuation orders covered parts of Pemberton and Lil’wat Nation on Thursday, Nov. 12. Some areas received more than 300 millimetres of rain in 48 hours, and floodwater closed Highway 99 east of Pemberton and roads near Squamish. The entire Village of Pemberton was under an evacuation alert. Evacuation orders also remained in effect in Zeballos, where flooding and landslide risks threatened about 30 properties. The release of water from the Cheakamus Dam flooded roads near Squamish and was intended to make room in the reservoir for more rain. Officials expected river levels to crest Thursday and then recede. Rain eased in some areas, but Vancouver Island remained under rainfall and flood warnings, and forecasters were tracking more storm systems expected over the weekend.

items.title: [tsln.com] Cattle specialists urge targeted winter feeding to manage costs
items.content_html:
🌲 ✏️

Cattle advisers and researchers are urging producers to match winter rations to forage quality and herd needs. Drought has tightened forage supplies, and feed is a major operating expense. South Dakota State University research found that limit-fed, energy-dense diets reduced feed use and methane emissions without harming calf growth through weaning, saving about $29 per cow. Kansas State University cow-calf specialist Jason Warner recommends assessing forage and supplementing protein as dormant grasses lose quality. French livestock trainer Guillaume Beaure describes reducing feed waste by closely matching rations to animals’ needs. Advisers also recommend checking forage mineral levels because winter hay can pose a risk of magnesium deficiency.

items.title: [phys.org] COP31 nations split over 1.5°C goal as threshold nears
items.content_html:
🌲 ✏️

Halfway through the COP31 climate negotiations in Antalya, countries are divided over whether to keep the 1.5°C warming limit as a central goal after the United Nations said in September that crossing it was imminent and unavoidable. Global temperatures have risen about 1.4°C above pre-industrial levels. Some countries want the summit’s final decision to reaffirm 1.5°C as the “right goal” and call for temperatures to return below that limit as soon as possible. Other negotiators, including members of the Arab Group and Like-Minded Developing Countries, are pushing to weaken or remove references to the target. Scientists say reversing an overshoot would require sharp emissions cuts and large-scale carbon removal over decades; University of Exeter climate scientist Pierre Friedlingstein described that prospect as “extremely ambitious”.

items.title: [winnipegfreepress.com] Federal memo warns freshwater pressures threaten Canada’s long-term security
items.content_html:
🌲 ✏️

An internal federal memo warns that growing pressure on freshwater supplies could harm Canada’s long-term security and prosperity. It says it is unclear whether the country can meet future needs as its cities and economy grow. The Canada Water Agency prepared the document for Environment Minister Julie Dabrusin as work proceeds on a national water security strategy. Dabrusin called the strategy a “mission critical priority” in response to Prime Minister Mark Carney’s request for cabinet priorities. The memo links water risks to climate change, pollution, population growth, overuse and aging infrastructure. Public consultation ran from Sept. 9 to Oct. 25, and the agency also consulted provincial, territorial and Indigenous partners. The memo calls for an assessment of water protection and sustainable management, including shared waters with the United States and global water risks. The 12-page memo was obtained through an access-to-information request, with some material withheld.

The U.S. National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration’s (NOAA) Climate Prediction Center said the developing El Niño is likely to remain strong to very strong through March 2027, with ocean temperatures still rising. The event is already associated with unusually warm waters off California, higher coastal water levels and changes in marine food supplies. Scientists report seabirds washing ashore and kelp forests under stress. The pattern can shift rainfall and temperature, and forecasters expect warmer winters in the Northwest that could reduce snowpack by raising snow levels. Scientists also warn that warm Pacific waters can increase the risk of coastal flooding when high tides coincide with storms. items.content_html:

A groundbreaking drone survey has revealed a startling split in the fate of New Zealand's endangered Erect-crested penguins. While one population has remained stable for decades, another has declined by more than 40%, apparently due to a combination of predators, worsening storms, and changing ocean conditions. Even more surprisingly, the tiny Bounty Islands support nearly as many breeding pairs as the Antipodes Islands, despite being 40 times smaller.

items.title: [phys.org] UN warns warming will breach 1.5C as COP31 opens Monday
items.content_html:
🌲 ✏️

The United Nations says global warming will exceed the 1.5-degree Celsius threshold as nearly 200 countries prepare to begin the COP31 climate talks in Antalya, Turkey, on Nov. 9. Climate scientists say the rate of warming has effectively doubled over the past decade. October 2026 was the hottest October on record, and 2026 is virtually certain to become the second year to exceed 1.5C, after 2024. U.N. Secretary-General António Guterres said the world must now limit how far temperatures rise beyond that level and blamed political leaders for failing to act. The Nov. 9-20 talks are expected to focus on fulfilling earlier promises to move away from fossil fuels and on funding for poorer countries facing climate impacts. Turkey is promoting a goal to increase electricity’s share of global energy demand from about 20% to 35% by 2035. Developed countries have resisted further funding commitments, and the Trump administration is not taking part in negotiations.

items.title: [livescience.com] NASA's Swift telescope burns up after nearly 22 years
items.content_html:
🌲 ✏️

NASA’s Neil Gehrels Swift Observatory reentered Earth’s atmosphere and burned up over North Sumatra on Nov. 4, ending a nearly 22-year mission. Its observations, including millions of images, remain available for research. A 24-hour ultraviolet exposure of the Andromeda galaxy was assembled from observations made between May and July 2008. NASA said Swift detected about 20,000 ultraviolet sources there, many of them hot stars and star clusters obscured in visible-light views. Swift was designed to turn rapidly toward short-lived cosmic explosions and observe them in optical, ultraviolet and X-ray light. It also alerted other observatories so they could follow events before they faded. The U.S. Space Force said Swift reentered the atmosphere at 7:39 a.m. EST over North Sumatra. NASA expected most of the spacecraft to burn up, though some pieces may have survived.

items.title: [scimex.org] Astronomers trace eight-minute radio pulses to white dwarf and Sun-like star
items.content_html:
🌲 ✏️

Astronomers have traced repeating radio pulses from the system GPM J071507−114153 to a white dwarf orbiting a Sun-like star—the first known long-period radio transient with this type of stellar pairing. The pulses recur every 7.9 minutes but appear only during a roughly six-hour window in each 32-hour orbit. The system lies more than 5,000 light-years away. Researchers discovered the system using Australia’s Murchison Widefield Array, pinpointed it with South Africa’s MeerKAT telescope and used the W. M. Keck Observatory in Hawaii to identify the companion as a G-type star. Measurements of the orbit and the companion’s slight movement indicate that the pulsing object has about two-thirds the Sun’s mass, making it too light to be a neutron star. The study was published in Nature Astronomy on Nov. 12, 2026.

The preliminary government figures marked the first contraction in four quarters. Private consumption fell 0.3%, while higher energy import costs also weighed on activity. The government is considering a food tax cut, but financing remains uncertain because of concerns over rising public debt and how to replace the revenue. Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi said the government would continue price support and work to foster wage increases. The Bank of Japan’s next policy meeting is scheduled for Dec. 17-18, and weak consumption could divide policymakers over further rate increases.

items.title: [3dprinting.com] 3D-printed tungsten tiles withstand 74 plasma discharges in fusion test
items.content_html:
🌲 ✏️

Full-size 3D-printed tungsten tiles survived 74 plasma discharges inside the DIII-D National Fusion Facility in San Diego, remaining intact after about four minutes of total plasma exposure over three days. The test subjected industrial-scale printed components to conditions relevant to fusion-reactor hardware, including intense heat and particle bombardment. Researchers from North Carolina State University, Oak Ridge National Laboratory and Japanese manufacturer JEOL made the tiles using electron-beam powder bed fusion, keeping the tungsten powder bed above 1,400°C during printing to limit cracking. The parts still await detailed erosion and surface analysis after a radiation survey.

items.title: [space.com] Simulations link Uranus and Neptune’s skewed magnetic fields to interior conditions
items.content_html:
🌲 ✏️

Computer simulations based on Voyager 2 measurements suggest that increasing electrical conductivity with depth inside Uranus and Neptune may explain their unusually tilted, off-center magnetic fields. The study, led by Chi Yan of the University of Texas at Austin, was published Nov. 3 in Communications Physics. The models indicate that the fields may also shift substantially over decades, unlike Earth’s comparatively steady magnetic tilt. Researchers are using observations of faint auroras from the James Webb Space Telescope to track the planets’ magnetic environments; NASA has prioritized a Uranus mission for the early 2040s.

items.title: [arstechnica.com] FAA plans to replace floppy-based air traffic systems by 2028
items.content_html:
🌲 ✏️

The Federal Aviation Administration plans to replace four aging information systems that rely on floppy disks with a unified digital platform at 435 air traffic facilities by the end of 2028. The new Enterprise Information Display System, or E-IDS, will consolidate weather alerts, airport status and flight notices that controllers currently retrieve through outdated, often manual processes. The FAA says the platform will give controllers faster access to safety-critical information and reduce maintenance problems. The agency has already upgraded five sites, while Congress has provided $12.5 billion for broader air traffic control modernization. The FAA is seeking additional funding through the proposed Modern Skies Act. The agency plans to deploy the system at the remaining locations by the end of 2028.

Democrats won control of both chambers of Congress in the Nov. 3 midterm elections, flipping Senate seats in states including Texas, Ohio, Kansas and South Carolina. With 228 House seats and 54 Senate seats reported for the party, Democrats will control committees and confirmation votes when the new Congress convenes in January. President Donald Trump retains the power to veto legislation and direct executive policy. Voters’ concerns about living costs, inflation, tariffs and the Iran war contributed to Republican losses. The conflict, launched in February, drove fuel prices higher; U.S. inflation stood at 3.7% before the election. Markets initially wavered, then rallied on Nov. 4: the Dow rose 3%, while Brent crude fell 8.7% to $94.62 a barrel as investors reassessed the risk of prolonged conflict and political uncertainty. The new Congress also faces a Dec. 11 deadline to authorize government spending. Analysts expect legislative gridlock, and Trump may retain his executive authority to impose tariffs.

items.title: [sciencefeatured.com] Higher BMI over time linked to faster cognitive decline in older adults
items.content_html:
🌲 ✏️

A 24-year study of several thousand middle-aged and older Americans found that higher average body mass index (BMI) over time was associated with faster declines in memory and thinking. A team led by University of Georgia researcher Suhang Song reported the findings in the Journal of Neurology. The association was strongest when cognitive abilities were assessed about eight years after weight measurements and was more pronounced among participants who were older when the study began. The observational study cannot establish that higher weight causes cognitive decline or that weight loss would prevent it. The researchers noted that participants reported their own height and weight and that the analysis could not account for physical activity. The team called for further research into possible biological mechanisms and future interventions.

items.content_html:
🌲 ✏️

Russia launched 172 drones and 36 ballistic missiles at Kyiv and surrounding areas overnight on Nov. 6-7, damaging energy infrastructure, homes, a kindergarten and the Northern Bridge, Ukrainian authorities said. Authorities reported at least one person killed and eight wounded. Russia’s Defense Ministry said it struck military-industrial, energy and transport targets and claimed the bridge was used to move weapons and military equipment. Strikes hit substations that carry electricity from the Rivne and Khmelnytskyi nuclear power plants to Kyiv and central Ukraine; other substations were damaged across five regions. Kyiv faced disruptions to electricity, heating and water as temperatures neared freezing, while the bridge was closed in both directions for assessment and repairs. Ukraine’s energy ministry said outages affected consumers in five regions and warned that continuing air-raid alerts were complicating repairs. President Volodymyr Zelenskyy accused Moscow of striking critical infrastructure to pressure Ukraine ahead of U.S.-brokered talks with Russia, scheduled for Nov. 10-11 in Abu Dhabi. The meeting will be the fourth round of talks brokered by the Trump administration. Earlier discussions produced no breakthrough, with territory and security guarantees among the unresolved issues.

items.title: [blog.ovhcloud.com] PHP hosting provider backports fixes across six million sites as patching lags
items.content_html:
🌲 ✏️

Hosting provider OVHcloud says it deployed official fixes or its own backports across all 15 PHP versions on its shared-hosting platform, covering more than 6 million websites on about 5,000 servers. The fixes address two PHP flaws collectively known as PHP2Shell that can let attackers run commands on vulnerable servers without credentials. The U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) has confirmed active exploitation and set an Oct. 29 deadline for federal civilian agencies to address the flaws. Censys’ tracker showed more than 10 million services patched since Oct. 21, while a scan found more than 4 million services in Germany still reporting vulnerable PHP version numbers. The scanner cautions that backported fixes may not appear in those version strings. OVHcloud says it wrote fixes for PHP 5.3 through 7.3, versions the PHP project no longer maintains. Researchers documented 35 shell executions on three deliberately vulnerable honeypots, but the test used a favorable single-worker setup. CISA has not named affected organizations or described the evidence behind its listing, and the designation does not establish the scale of successful compromises in production. Some earlier claims of successful exploitation were withdrawn or qualified after investigators found scanning or could not confirm PHP2Shell as the entry point.

items.title: [cbc.ca] Canadian police suspend use of Crime Stoppers after 1.5 million records exposed
items.content_html:
🌲 ✏️

Canadian police services are suspending their use of Crime Stoppers after a breach exposed more than 1.5 million tips submitted across Canada over 25 years, a CBC News investigation found. More than 850,000 records included personally identifiable information. The tips were managed through P3, software provided by U.S.-based Navigate360. Navigate360 acknowledged on Friday that its database had been breached between November 2025 and March 2026 and said potentially exposed information included names, addresses, birth dates and Social Security numbers. The company said it had no evidence the information had been used for fraud or identity theft. Police in several provinces have paused their use of the service while they assess the breach and its safeguards. Toronto and Ottawa police are directing people to report information through police channels, which do not necessarily offer the same anonymity. Crime Stoppers chapters and police are seeking further details from Navigate360. The company said it hired a cybersecurity firm to help strengthen security.

items.title: [thestar.com] Supreme Court hears challenge to Canada’s ban on 2,500 firearm types
items.content_html:
🌲 ✏️

The Supreme Court of Canada began hearing a challenge Monday to the federal ban on more than 2,500 types of firearms the government classifies as assault-style weapons. The appeal follows two lower-court defeats for gun owners, advocacy groups and businesses challenging cabinet’s authority to prohibit the guns through regulations. The ban includes some firearms used for hunting and sport shooting. The government prohibited 1,500 models and variants, including the AR-15 and Ruger Mini-14, in May 2020 and later expanded the list. Federal lawyers argue cabinet acted reasonably to address public-safety risks, while appellants say the regulations exceeded the authority Parliament granted and failed to account for lawful sporting and hunting uses. The hearings continue Tuesday, and a decision is expected by the end of 2027 at the latest. The possession amnesty runs until 90 days after the court rules.

items.content_html:
🌲 ✏️

Children and young adults with atopic dermatitis had 28% higher odds of sleep disturbance than peers without the condition, a retrospective review of 26,395 patients at an urban primary care clinic found. The association remained after researchers accounted for coexisting atopy and mental health conditions; neither significantly changed the link. The study included patients aged 0 to 21; 14.5% had atopic dermatitis and 10.3% had sleep disturbance. Samantha Sundermeier, DO, an attending physician at Children’s Hospital of Philadelphia, said future studies should assess disease severity, treatment response and sleep over time using validated measures and patient-reported outcomes.
